items.followUp: Define root hairs and state how they help a plant absorb water and minerals.

rubric.why: Identifies what root hairs are and where they occur.
rubric.description: Root hairs are tiny tubular extensions of root epidermal cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as extensions of root epidermal cells.

rubric.why: States the function of root hairs.
rubric.description: They increase the root’s surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts from the soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining their role in absorption.

modelAnswer: Root hairs are tiny tubular extensions of the epidermal cells of roots.
They increase the root’s surface area and absorb water and mineral salts from the soil.

items.followUp: What is a cell? State why it is called the basic unit of life.

rubric.why: Explains the meaning and function of an organelle.
rubric.description: An organelle is a specialised structure within a cell that performs a particular function; for example, mitochondria release energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an organelle as a specialised cell structure and 1 mark for its specific function or a valid example.

rubric.why: Describes the cell level of organisation.
rubric.description: At the cell level, organelles work together within a cell, the basic structural and functional unit of life.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the cell as the basic unit of life and 1 mark for explaining that its organelles work together.

modelAnswer: At the organelle level, specialised structures within a cell perform particular functions; for example, mitochondria release energy.
At the cell level, organelles work together to carry out life processes.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

items.followUp: Name the two main complex tissues in plants and state the function of each.

accept: more than one type of cell
rubric.why: Defines a compound tissue.
rubric.description: A compound tissue consists of more than one type of cell working together to perform a common function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining compound tissue as different cell types working together.

rubric.why: Identifies xylem and its transport role, with its components as supporting detail.
rubric.description: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots; it includes vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transport function and 1 mark for naming xylem or its components.

rubric.why: Identifies phloem and its transport role, with its components as supporting detail.
rubric.description: Phloem transports prepared food through the plant; it includes sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the transport function and 1 mark for naming phloem or its components.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues are made of more than one type of cell working together to perform a common function.
Xylem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to other parts of the plant.
Xylem is composed of vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
Phloem transports prepared food from one part of the plant to other parts.
Phloem is composed of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.

items.followUp: Explain how light energy is absorbed and used during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Identifies chlorophyll and its location.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll is the green pigment present in chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chlorophyll as the green pigment in chloroplasts.

rubric.why: States chlorophyll’s role in capturing light.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs or traps light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs or traps light.

rubric.why: Explains the role of light as the energy source.
rubric.description: Light supplies the energy needed for photosynthesis; photosynthesis cannot proceed normally without light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light as the energy source or stating its necessity.

rubric.why: Connects absorbed light energy to the production of food.
rubric.description: The absorbed energy is converted into chemical energy and used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that light energy is converted or used to produce food.

rubric.why: Adds a relevant textbook detail about light or chlorophyll.
rubric.description: The rate of photosynthesis is affected by light intensity; chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid detail about light intensity or the wavelengths absorbed/reflected.

modelAnswer: Chlorophyll is the green pigment found in chloroplasts.
It absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis.
Light provides the energy for photosynthesis, and its intensity affects the rate of the process.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy and used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue light and reflects green light.

items.followUp: Describe how sugars move from a source to a sink through phloem by the pressure-flow mechanism.

rubric.why: Identifies sugar loading at the source.
rubric.description: Sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem at the source, such as a photosynthesising leaf.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugar is loaded into phloem at the source.

rubric.why: Explains water entry and pressure rise at the source.
rubric.description: Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, increasing hydrostatic pressure at the source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water entry by osmosis or the resulting pressure rise.

rubric.why: Explains movement of phloem sap down a pressure gradient.
rubric.description: The pressure difference causes phloem sap to move by mass flow from the source towards the sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking a pressure gradient to mass flow.

rubric.why: Describes sugar unloading and use at the sink.
rubric.description: Sugars are unloaded at the sink, where they are used or stored.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugar is unloaded at the sink and giving its use or storage.

rubric.why: Completes the pressure-flow cycle at the sink.
rubric.description: Water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, lowering pressure at the sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing water return to the xylem or the lower pressure at the sink.

modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem.
Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, raising the hydrostatic pressure at the source.
The pressure difference causes phloem sap to flow by mass flow towards a sink.
At the sink, sugars are unloaded and are used or stored.
Water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, so pressure is lower at the sink.

rubric.why: Defines histology.
rubric.description: Histology is the study of tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining histology as the study of tissues.

rubric.why: Defines physiology.
rubric.description: Physiology is the study of the functions of living organisms and their parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining physiology as the study of functions.

modelAnswer: Histology is the study of tissues.
Physiology is the study of the functions of living organisms and their parts.

items.followUp: What is a colonial type of cellular organisation? Give one example.

rubric.why: Describes the arrangement of cells in a colony.
rubric.description: In colonial organisation, cells of the same species live together in a group or colony.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cells of the same species living together as a colony.

rubric.why: States a feature or example of colonial organisation.
rubric.description: The cells generally retain their independence and can perform life functions; Volvox is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid feature of the cells or the example Volvox.

modelAnswer: In colonial type cellular organisation, cells of the same species live together in a colony.
The cells retain a degree of independence and can perform life functions; Volvox is an example.

items.followUp: What is a biological problem, and how may it arise during an investigation?

rubric.why: Defines a biological problem.
rubric.description: A biological problem is a question about living organisms or a biological phenomenon that needs investigation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an investigable question about biology.

rubric.why: Explains how a biological problem is identified.
rubric.description: It commonly arises from observations that lead to a question requiring investigation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the problem to an observation or the need for investigation.

modelAnswer: A biological problem is a question about living organisms or a biological phenomenon that needs investigation.
It may arise from observations that lead to a question requiring further study.
